sentences.text: The name Clidastes means "locked vertebrae," derived from the Greek word for key, referring to vertebral processes that interlock to provide stability and strength while swimming.
This animal had a narrow head and slender body, giving it a very hydrodynamic shape.
It possessed a delicate, slim form with expanded neural spines and chevrons near the tail tip, enabling it to chase fast prey.
Mosasaur teeth, including those of Clidastes, typically have a pointed, curved crown sitting on a bony pedicel.
The marginal tooth rows in Clidastes are located on the premaxilla, maxilla, and dentary.
The premaxillary suture of the maxilla was smoothly keeled and parallel to the longitudinal axis, with sixteen to eighteen teeth in the maxilla.
Specimens found in Kansas revealed humeri and femora with round heads, a feature similar to mammals.
Good preservation allowed researchers to note that chevrons were ankylosed to the center of the vertebrae, a trait not seen in other mosasaurs.
The initial specimens found included a juvenile, representing one of the best-preserved and most complete mosasaurs from Alabama.
The genus Clidastes was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1868.
The first specimens of Clidastes propython were discovered by E. D. Cope in 1869 in the Mooreville Chalk of Lowndes County, Alabama.
Additional remains of Clidastes were found in Kansas by Charles H. Sternberg and his son in 1918.
Clidastes liodontus was described from the Smoky Hill Chalk Member of the Niobrara Formation in Kansas.
Clidastes was likely an agile swimmer that hunted cephalopods, fish, and small vertebrates in shallow waters.
Isotopic analysis of teeth suggests Clidastes may have occasionally entered freshwater, similar to modern sea snakes.
They are not considered very agile because their flippers were not fully webbed.
They possessed nerve branches extending to the tip of the tail, which would allow them to beat the water to move at high speeds.
Clidastes is firmly placed in the subfamily Mosasaurinae due to its dental and vertebral morphology being closer to Mosasaurus than any other mosasaur.
Clidastes is often recovered as a basal mosasaurine and the most basal hydropedal mosasaurine genus, more derived than Dallasaurus but less derived than Prognathodon or Globidens.
Currently, only one species, C. propython, is considered valid within the genus Clidastes.
C. iguanavus was the original type species, but C. propython was designated the new type species by the ICZN in 1993 based on diagnostic remains because it is the best studied.
C. iguanavus is the original type species of Clidastes but is poorly known compared to other species.
C. iguanavus can be differentiated by kidney-shaped central articulations and stout centrum proportions.
Fossils of Clidastes date from the Coniacian to the Campanian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
Clidastes lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America.
The genus existed from the Turonian to the Maastrichtian, between 93.9 and 66 million years ago.
The species lived from the middle Santonian to the Middle to Late Campanian, coinciding with an extinction event that heavily affected Clidastes.
Specimens have been referred to this genus from marine deposits in Sweden, Germany, Russia, Mexico, and Jordan.
Lively (2019) declared C. liodontus a nomen dubium and recommended restricting the genus to C. propython.
Lively (2019) questioned the referral of remains from outside the US to Clidastes due to their fragmentary nature.
